extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of comedy/pop culture (particularly SNL history)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points about when a comedian/host is appropriate for a mainstream sketch show (SNL), how to judge controversial material, and how cast members might respond to morally objectionable hosts. Draws on Nora Dunn's 1990 boycott and later reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting as endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: “having someone as the host isn’t ‘examining’ them, it’s endorsing them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nora Dunn argues that putting someone on as host signals endorsement rather than neutral examination; producers should recognize that booking a host can be read as institutional approval and carries ethical weight. ('You’re endorsing them. ... You can’t put something like that on.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid punching down
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy that 'punches down' on the most vulnerable is irresponsible and harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece cites criticism (even from George Carlin) of Andrew Dice Clay for using comedy 'to punch down on those most vulnerable.' Such material provokes revulsion and can legitimize hateful attitudes; comedians and shows should avoid amplifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody defense fails if audience agrees with hateful persona
rubrics_metrics.description: “I know he says he’s doing a parody, but the laughs are coming because they love that character and they agree with that character. He was Andrew Dice Clay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience is cheering and identifying with the hateful character rather than seeing it as critical satire, invoking 'parody' does not excuse the content. Evaluate audience reaction when judging whether material is satirical or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial characters must be challenged in-performance (Archie Bunker model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archie Bunker was acceptable because 'there was another voice... Archie was challenged all the time' — controversial figures can be part of discussion when counterpoints are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A controversial or offensive character can be framed responsibly if sketches include voices that challenge the viewpoint and create a critical discussion; merely presenting a hateful persona without pushback is problematic ('Andrew Dice Clay isn’t a discussion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast response: refuse to perform with objectionable hosts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a host is morally objectionable, a cast member should 'don’t do it. Just say, "I’m not doing it."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nora presents refusal to perform as a legitimate tactic (her own boycott, Sinéad O’Connor joining after hearing Dice's material). This is proposed as an ethical stance performers can take, though it may carry consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for professional consequences of protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Nora Dunn reports long-term penalties: being excluded from tributes, reduced billing/pay, and lack of contact from producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that public protest can lead to reputational or career costs (e.g., not being rehired, being seated separately at anniversary events, lower pay for offered work). Performers should weigh ethical stands against potential fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producers often prioritize ratings/controversy when choosing hosts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Why do you think controversial figures ... are asked to be hosts? It's the ratings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booking decisions can be driven by audience numbers and 'cutting edge' appeal rather than ethical fit; this is an implicit selection criterion of producers to be aware of when evaluating host appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure writers create material for all cast members (avoid sidelining women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nora: 'We’re women, and the guys don’t write for us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial and writing practices should include material tailored to the diversity of the cast; otherwise certain performers (e.g., women) may be consistently marginalized and underused in sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't hire or endorse personalities who promote hate or target vulnerable minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: On later controversial hires (e.g., Dave Chappelle, Trump), Nora: 'You can’t endorse that. ... I don’t think he should have been hired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a performer’s recent material actively targets and denigrates small or vulnerable groups, hiring them for mainstream platforms is ethically questionable. The piece treats such hiring as an endorsement and advises against it.
